Q: Optional logging with a writer monad in haskell A:

WriterT is very bad for logs. Unless you're importing the .CPS module, it's literally impossible to make it not generate nested thunks. In either case, it's impossible to use it to log eagerly - the shape of the data type m (a, w) requires the m action to be run before the log is available. You might be able to consume it incrementally with a sufficiently lazy monad instance, but IO and types based on it are not that lazy.

I really think it's a mistake for the documentation for Writer to mention logging. The expectations people have for log behavior generally can't be met by the type. It does have some use cases where you always want the full result at the end of the action, but it's super niche. I'd avoid it unless you understand its operational limitations in detail and know you're in a case where they don't matter and are unlikely to matter as the code evolves.

Q: Combine the output of proc freq A:

CATS will remove all spaces. CATX will let you put arbitrary delimiters in between:

myval = cats(N, "    (   ", put(Percent, 5.1), "% ) ");

gives 3(15%) no matter how many spaces you put.

myval = catx(" ",N,catx("  ","(", cats(put(Percent, 5.1), "%)")));

will give 3 ( 15%)

Note you have to use one CATS for the "15%)", one CATX with two spaces to create "( 15%)", and one CATX for the final space after 3.

Q: T-SQL: Calculating the Nth Percentile Value from column A:

If you want to get exactly the 90th percentile value, excluding NULLs, I would suggest doing the calculation directly. The following version calculates the row number and number of rows, and selects the appropriate value:

select max(case when rownum*1.0/numrows <= 0.9 then colA end) as percentile_90th
from (select colA,
             row_number() over (order by colA) as rownum,
             count(*) over (partition by NULL) as numrows
      from t
      where colA is not null
     ) t

I put the condition in the SELECT clause rather than the WHERE clause, so you can easily get the 50th percentile, 17th, or whatever values you want.

Q: Pascal decimal-point A:

To solve the 3rd point: think about x and y as about a fraction. Here is the basic idea:

  1. A           := A / GCD(A, B);
B           := B / GCD(A, B)

  2. integerPart := A div B;
A           := A mod B
  3. Non‐periodical part: 
    while A mod 2 = 0 do
BEGIN
    C := C*2;
    A := A div 2
END;

while A mod 5 = 0 do
BEGIN
    C := C * 5;
    A := A div 5
END
  4. Find M so that A * M = 999…999.

Q: VB.NET SQL select columns and display in grid A:

Since you initialize Dim sr As New StreamReader(sPath), sr will not be Nothing. The check If (sr IsNot Nothing) is unnecessary.

But instead you should read sString before you test it for Nothing. You can do this with an infinite loop and exit the loop when the string becomes Nothing

Dim sr As New StreamReader(sPath)

Do While True
    sString = sr.ReadLine
    If sString Is Nothing Then
        Exit Do
    End If
    'TODO: do something with sString
Loop

You could also simplify all the database related stuff by using an O/R-mapper like Dapper (simple) or EF Core (complex, but powerful). This in conjunction with data binding will also simplify your DataGridView code. Well, it will more or less eliminate it.

See also: ASPSnippets – Bind DataGridView using Dapper (C# & VB.NET).

But you can also load the data into a business class instead of using a DataTable. i didn't find good examples in VB. If you can read C#, you will find a lot more examples.

Q: Why does non-equality check of one variable against many values always return true? A:

Use &&/AND/and, not ||/OR/or:

v != "x" && v != "y" && v != "z"

Problem

If an if block is always executed, the condition for the if block always evaluates to true. The logical expression must be wrong.

Let us consider v != "x" || v != "y" || v != "z" for each value of v.

  • When v = "x",

    v != "x" becomes "x" != "x", which is false.
    v != "y" becomes "x" != "y", which is true.
    v != "z" becomes "x" != "z", which is true.

    The expression evaluates to false || true || true, which is true.

  • When v = "y", the expression becomes

      "y" != "x" || "y" != "y" || "y" != "z"

    or true || false || true, which is true.

  • When v = "z", the expression becomes

      "z" != "x" || "z" != "y" || "z" != "z"

    or true || true || false, which is true.

  • For any other value for v, the expression evaluates to true || true || true, which is true.

Alternatively, consider the truth-table:

       │     A          B          C      │
  v    │  v != "x"   v != "y"   v != "z"  │  A || B || C
───────┼──────────────────────────────────┼──────────────
 "x"   │    false      true       true    │     true
 "y"   │    true       false      true    │     true
 "z"   │    true       true       false   │     true
other  │    true       true       true    │     true

As you can see, your logical expression always evaluates to true.

Solution

What you want to do is, find a logical expression that evaluates to true when

(v is not "x")and(v is not "y")and(v is not "z").

The correct construction is,

  • for C-like languages (e.g., C#, JavaScript-(may need the strict equality operator !==), and PHP)

      if (v != "x" && v != "y" && v != "z")
  {
      // the statements I want to be executed
      // if v is neither "x", nor "y", nor "z"
  }

  • for Pascal-like languages (PL/SQL is syntactically similar)

      IF (v != 'x' AND v != 'y' AND v != 'z') THEN
      -- the statements I want to be executed
      -- if v is neither "x", nor "y", nor "z"
  END IF;

De Morgan's law

By De Morgan's law, the expression can also be rewritten as (using C-like syntax)

!(v == "x" || v == "y" || v == "z")

meaning

not((v is "x")or(v is "y")or(v is "z")).

This makes the logic a bit more obvious.

Specific languages

Some languages have specific constructs for testing membership in sets, or you can use array/list operations.

  • SQL: v NOT IN ('x', 'y', 'z')

  • JavaScript: !["x", "y", "z"].includes(v)

  • Python: v not in {"x", "y", "z"}

  • Java: !Arrays.asList("x", "y", "z").contains(v)

  • Java 9 (and above): !Set.of("x", "y", "z").contains(v)
